title: Bandwidth fencing for prefill/decode with sparse-attention kernel hints
creator: Aisha Banerjee
description: Introduce a lightweight bandwidth-fencing layer in the prefill/decode scheduler that enforces soft throughput caps per tenant/priority-band while using sparse-attention signals to bias kernel selection toward fast sparse kernels when safe. The goal is to reduce tail latency and tenant-induced starvation without sacrificing overall throughput for bursty workloads.
background: We've observed recurring microburst-induced tail latency where large prefill+decode flows from a single tenant monopolize fast kernels and memory bandwidth, delaying smaller latency-sensitive requests. Existing phase-splitting heuristics prioritize fairness by token-phase quotas but still allow kernel-level contention. Parallel work on kernel hinting (ENG-82314, ENG-52678) shows that sparse-attention-compatible kernels can be substantially faster in some models, but we currently don't expose a routing mechanism to leverage that signal in scheduling.
proposal: Add a 'bandwidth fence' abstraction to the request router that tracks a moving window of GPU bandwidth usage (bytes/sec and active WMs) per tenant and per priority band. When a band approaches its soft cap, the scheduler will: 1) preferentially split prefill phases into finer-grained micro-phases to interleave with other tenants; 2) steer eligible requests to sparse-attention kernels by honoring a new kernel_hint field in the request metadata; 3) apply lightweight backpressure (10-30ms) or fast-path demotion to lower-cost model variants. The fence is soft: it only influences scheduling decisions and hedging, not hard-rejects traffic.
design_notes: Bandwidth metric = combined read/write memory bytes + SM occupancy estimate from kernel telemetry aggregated over 1s sliding window.
Kernel hinting: add kernel_hint enum {auto, dense_fast, sparse_fast, legacy} in internal routing header; default auto uses model heuristics and historical telemetry.
Micro-phase splitting uses a bounded token slice size (configurable 8-64 tokens) with a per-request max-splits cap to limit overhead.
Fence thresholds: default soft cap per tenant = 60% of a GPU's sustained bandwidth share for high-priority tenants, 30% for low-priority.
We will keep tenant credit bookkeeping in the existing QoS store; no new external stateful service required.
Compatibility: fall back to existing phase-splitting if kernel_hint cannot be honored (e.g., model incompatible with sparse kernels).
Expose observability: new console charts for bandwidth usage, kernel_hint acceptance rate, and micro-phase overheads.
experiments: Experiment A: 3-day alpha on a dedicated pool with mixed workloads (50% latency-sensitive chat, 50% high-throughput batch) comparing baseline vs bandwidth-fence with kernel_hints enabled. KPI: 99th pct latency for chat flows.
Experiment B: synthetic worst-case tenant hammer test to validate fence prevents starvation and observes graceful degradation under sustained pressure.
Experiment C: A/B test of micro-phase granularity (8/16/32 tokens) to find optimal split size vs overhead tradeoff.
Failure modes to monitor: increased total tokens/sec overhead due to micro-slicing, kernel hint misclassification causing quality regressions, and telemetry lag leading to oscillation.
metrics: Primary: chat 99th percentile latency (ms) under mixed load
Secondary: total tokens/sec per GPU, mean latency, kernel_hint acceptance rate, micro-phase CPU overhead (ms/request), model quality regression delta (embedding/text gen BLEU/ROUGE proxy)
SLO targets: maintain baseline throughput within -8% and reduce 99p latency for P0 flows by >=20% in alpha pool
rollout_plan: Phase 0 (canary): Implement feature-flagged routing and telemetry stubs; run internal unit tests and local integration. (1 week)
Phase 1 (alpha): Enable on dedicated alpha pool with small set of tenants; run Experiments A/B/C; collect metrics and iterate. (2 weeks)
Phase 2 (beta): Expand to mixed-hosted pools with opt-in via tenant config; add console charts and cost breakdowns. (2-3 weeks)
Phase 3 (GA): Enable by default with conservative thresholds and provide customer docs + migration guide. (dependent on experiment results)

tradeoffs: Micro-splitting reduces tail latency by enabling interleaving, but increases per-request overhead (extra scheduling and kernel launches). We cap splits to bound overhead.

Biasing toward sparse kernels improves latency for compatible models but risks quality regressions if the sparse kernel implementation has subtle differences; we only hint when model telemetry shows compatibility and include a rollback path.
Soft fencing trades absolute throughput for predictability. We prefer soft influence over hard rejects to avoid surprising customers, at cost of slightly lower utilization in edge cases.
qa_plan: Unit tests for fence bookkeeping, integration tests with synthetic multi-tenant load, regression test against baseline latency/throughput, and manual spot-checks for model output parity when sparse kernels are used.
